text:
Here are some questions you could talk about together:

Audience (who they were written for):

  • Who were the recipes written for?
  • What clues do they give about their audience?
  • What special features do they have for their particular audience?
  • Do they fit their audiences or do they need something else to help?


Look on the page:

  • Which recipe looks most attractive on the page? Why?
  • What organisational features do the recipes use?
  • How do the organisational features help the reader?
  • Is it easy to find information? Why or why not?
  • Is it easy to follow the steps in the recipe? Why or why not?


    • Look at the language (word choices) used:

  • Is it formal or informal?
  • Sometimes recipes can be quite chatty, other times they can be bossy, or something else. What are these recipes like?
  • Are there any tricky words? Does the recipe writer explain what they mean? Do they need to explain the words (think about the audience)?
  • Are the words written just to be useful or is there anything to make them fun to read as well as useful to cook?


    • Look at the steps in the recipe:

  • Are the sentences the same length in both recipes? Which is longer?
  • Do the steps contain information that you don’t actually need to be able to cook the recipe? Why? Is it helpful or unhelpful?
  • How do the steps begin – are there sentence openers? How do they help?


    • Deciding which you prefer:

    • Which recipe do you prefer? Why?
    • Do you think everyone would like the same one as you? Why?
    • Who might prefer the other one?
When you've finished writing your own recipe (Activity 2), compare it to the one you followed (Activity 1) and decide which you prefer and why.
